#### Abstract

This guideline advises on the management of patients with egg allergy. Most commonly egg allergy presents in infancy, with a prevalence of approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults. Following an acute allergic reaction, egg avoidance advice should be provided. Egg allergy usually resolves, and reintroduction can be achieved at home if reactions have been mild and there is no asthma. This is an update of the BSACI guideline for the management of egg allergy.1 It was prepared by an expert group of the Standards of Care Committee (SOCC) of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology (BSACI) and addresses the diagnosis and treatment of patients with egg allergy, for healthcare professionals working in secondary care.

This guideline focuses on type-1 IgE-mediated allergy to egg.
• The prevalence of egg allergy is estimated at approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults in the United Kingdom (Grade of recommendation = B).
• Allergic sensitization to egg, without a history of reacting, is common in infancy and should not prevent the introduction of egg into the diet, because this carries a risk of unnecessary dietary exclusion (Grade of recommendation =D).
• Egg allergy presents most commonly in infancy, usually after the first apparent ingestion, with rapid onset of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting (Grade of recommendation = B).
• Severe reactions involving respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms, presenting with cough, wheeze, breathing difficulty or pallor and floppiness are uncommon (Grade of recommendation = B).
• The clinical diagnosis is made by the rapid onset of typical symptoms (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg (Grade of recommendation = B).
• Reaction severity is related to the amount of egg ingested and the degree of cooking, with raw egg white being the most allergenic (Grade of recommendation =D).
• The presence of egg-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) or positive egg skin prick test (SPT) is useful in the management of moderatesevere cases or where there is diagnostic uncertainty (Grade of recommendation = B).
• The reported level of egg-specific IgE required to support a diagnosis varies between studies.

• An egg SPT weal of 3 mm or more in combination with a clinical history is considered adequate to confirm a diagnosis of egg allergy in most cases (Grade of recommendation = B).

• Most infants with egg allergy should continue to breastfeed, with their mother on an unrestricted diet (Grade of recommendation

= D).

• Referral to a dietician is needed for children with severe egg allergy for advice about strict egg avoidance (Grade of recommendation = D).

• If the history is unclear, a negative skin prick test can exclude egg allergy.

One death due to egg allergy has been reported in an adult patient in the UK since 1992.17,18 In children with eczema who are allergic to egg protein, dietary exclusion of egg results in improvement of their eczema.19 Clinical case examples of egg allergy presenting with varying degrees of severity are described in Appendix S1. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) is heat stable and immunodominant.2,3 The role of component allergens in predicting tolerance to baked egg white, or resolution of egg allergy in routine clinical practice has yet to be established.24 Persisting egg allergy is associated with a positive Gal d 1, and a level ≥11 kU/L indicates a high risk of reacting to cooked and raw egg.3 Gal d 1 is also a good indicator of whether the child is allergic only to raw egg, or to both cooked and raw egg.26 The acquisition of tolerance to egg is associated with a decrease in IgE to egg white and Gal d 1.27 When using test results to identify children at a high risk of anaphylaxis, although egg white sIgE levels are more sensitive, Gal d 1 has better positive predictive value and specificity.28 The current evidence suggests that egg components are rarely needed for the routine diagnosis and management of egg allergy in children but can be a useful adjunct for the assessment of egg allergy resolution in adults (Box 2). - 8.3 | Breastfeeding and egg allergy


Most breastfeeding mothers with egg-allergic children should continue to breastfeed on an unrestricted diet. Egg- allergic children have a two-fold increased risk of accidental reactions to egg, where there is no dietetic involvement in counselling the family.38 Dieticians provide valuable advice following hospital-based food challenges.

#### 8.6 | Provision of emergency medication and treatment plans

All families with egg-allergic children should have an appropriate oral antihistamine available, preferably a second generation, non-drowsy

- 9.1 | Prediction of resolution

At 1 year of age, complete resolution of egg allergy is more likely in children who can tolerate baked egg than those who continue to react.42 The phenotyping of egg allergy (baked egg tolerant vs. allergic) has prognostic implications and eases dietary restrictions.42 Children with mild/moderate egg allergy or with cutaneous reactions only are more likely to resolve.43

Persistence of egg allergy is associated with respiratory or multisystem symptoms, high egg specific IgE, presence of other food allergies or atopic co-morbidities.43–46 Sensitization to multiple egg allergen components, Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3 or Gal d 5, may identify children at risk of persistent egg allergy.47

- 9.2 | Natural history of resolution


Egg allergy resolves spontaneously in many affected children over several years, whereas in adults it tends to persist. Allergy to wellcooked egg resolves in about one third of children by 3 years of age, and two-thirds by 6 years (Figure 3).10 The rate of resolution varies between studies42,43,48,49 and egg allergy may continue until the teens.10 Systematic reviews suggest that the median age of resolution is 6–9 years, with 68% of egg-allergic individuals experiencing resolution by the age of 16 years.50

Tolerance to well-processed (baked or lightly cooked) egg occurs long before tolerance to uncooked egg (Figure 3). Children outgrow allergy to well-cooked egg approximately twice as quickly as they outgrow allergy to uncooked egg. Baked egg introduction improves quality of life for egg-allergic children, enhances the natural development of tolerance and de-restricts the diet.

If they react, they should be managed as egg allergic. #### 9.5 | Children with severe egg allergy

Children with severe egg allergy, severe multisystem allergic disease, faltering growth (Box 4) or egg allergy persisting beyond the time of usual resolution (6–7 years) should be followed up periodically to assess the likelihood of resolution and to refresh avoidance advice and emergency medication training. New onset adult egg allergy after eggs have been tolerated for years.71
- 2. Older children or adults with a pre-existing egg allergy, presenting to the adult clinic for the first time, should be assessed for the likely resolution of egg allergy. Although systematic review data suggest that 30% of egg-allergic children will continue to have persisting egg allergy after the age of 16 years, there are no data on continued resolution in young adults. Clinical experience shows that although it persists in some and may be lifelong, many others may have partly or wholly resolving egg allergy, even in their late 20' s. It is extremely important to establish the likelihood of tolerance with oral food challenges, as reactions can be severe and fatal anaphylaxis to egg has been reported in an adult patient.76

- 11 | OTHER EGG-RELATED CONDITIONS


- 11.1 | Egg allergy and asthma


Children with egg allergy are at increased risk of other allergic diseases especially asthma (odds ratio 5.0).77 A careful history should, therefore, be taken to enquire about respiratory symptoms. The presence of asthma may increase the potential severity

of accidental egg reactions and excellent asthma control should be a priority. It is safe to use and is recommended to be given to children with egg allergy in any setting, including primary care and schools76 (Department of health, 2017). Most adults and children with egg allergy can be safely immunized in primary care.

Investigation by measuring egg-specific IgE (by skin prick testing or specific IgE assay) is useful in moderate-severe cases or where there is diagnostic uncertainty. #### 2 | DEFINITION AND MECHANISM

Egg allergy is an adverse immunological reaction, most often induced by the proteins in egg white, usually ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and/ or ovomucoid (Gal d 1) mediated by egg-specific IgE. - 7.2 | Egg-specific IgE


When skin prick testing is not available, measurement of eggspecific IgE may be carried out in patients with a history of moderate/severe reactions to egg containing food, to confirm a clinical suspicion of egg allergy. Low levels of egg-specific IgE may be found in children without clinical egg allergy.13 The measurement of egg-specific IgE in the absence of a history of egg ingestion is discouraged as, in this circumstance, the test has poor specificity and low negative predictive value; cautious home introduction or oral challenge will subsequently be required if the egg-specific IgE level is positive but low.8 Measurement of peanut-specific IgE should be included in infants with moderate/severe egg allergy to guide peanut allergy prevention advice.25

#### 7.3 | Egg component testing

The egg white components are ovomucoid (Gal d 1), ovalbumin (Gal d 2), ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), lysozyme (Gal d 4) and livetin (Gal d 5). Adults with persistence of childhood egg allergy have more sequential than conformational IgE epitopes of ovomucoid.70

Yellow Fever vaccines should only be considered in egg-allergic patients under the guidance of an allergy specialist. This may be prevented by the early introduction of peanut into the diet (Grade of recommendation = B).
• New onset egg allergy in adults is rare; it is usually more severe and persists (Grade of recommendation = D).
• All children with egg allergy should receive the MMR immunization in primary care (Grade of recommendation = B).
• Children with egg allergy can receive the nasal live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) and most children and adults can receive the intramuscular influenza vaccine in primary care, unless they have had anaphylaxis to egg requiring admission to intensive care (Grade of recommendation = B).
• Yellow Fever vaccines contain detectable, but not quantified amounts of egg protein. If these vaccines are required, the eggallergic patient should be referred to an allergy specialist with access to a designated yellow fever vaccination centre for assessment and immunization (Grade of recommendation = B).

chunks.text:
Egg allergy most commonly presents after the first apparent ingestion.8,10,11 Most reactions occur to lightly cooked egg, with reactions to baked egg and raw egg being less common.10 Clinical reactions include urticaria and/or angio-oedema in 80–90% (within minutes) and gastrointestinal symptoms in 10–44% (within 2 h).10,12–14

Most reactions occurring in the community are mild, with facial erythema and/or urticaria. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg.

Moderate to severe reactions with respiratory symptoms are less common; 5–10% in challenge studies, but less in the community, where the initial triggering dose is usually lower.10,12,13 Prior to presentation to allergy services, anaphylaxis occurs in 7%.10

The severity of allergic reactions correlates with the amount of egg protein exposure15; as determined by the amount of egg protein ingested and the degree of processing (baked in wheat, cooked or raw, cooking duration and temperature). There are case reports of children who, following a negative cooked egg challenge, later have severe reactions to raw egg.56 Egg introduction or challenge should not be deferred for concern of increasing sensitization.43

Children undergoing hospital-based baked egg challenges rarely experience anaphylaxis requiring treatment with adrenaline; 2% in one study of 236 children.57 Adrenaline was not required in 181 hospital-based egg challenges.10

A recent study of 678 children undergoing hospital-based egg challenges identified two patients who satisfied BSACI criteria for home reintroduction, and experienced airway symptoms (personal communication – Aljneibi Shaikha). The risk of anaphylaxis in young children being given clear guidance on low-dose baked egg being gradually built up according to a ladder is minimal. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. Skin prick testing using a slurry of baked egg had a high negative predictive value for a negative baked egg challenge in one study.24 It is not routinely used in clinical practice.

chunks.text: SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23.

8 | MANAGEMENT

- 8.1 | Avoidance diets

Eggs served in a recognizable form are relatively easy to avoid. Individuals with severe egg allergy will need to completely avoid food sold loose/on buffets. Verbal and written advice on avoidance of egg products should be provided (see Appendices S2 and S3). Therefore, whilst the exclusion of eggs does not necessarily lead to nutritional deficiency, a registered dietician should be involved if the diet is also compromised by the exclusion of other foods due to multiple food allergies, lifestyle or religious reasons.37

Patients/families often wish to discuss avoidance in more detail, for example, with regard to specialist replacement products, recipes, eating out or management of children's parties.

#### 9.6 | Oral immunotherapy

Egg immunotherapy is a deliberate attempt, using regular ingestion of egg, usually with increasing amounts, to generate tolerance to egg in a patient with established egg allergy (usually over 5 years of age). Several studies have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of egg oral immunotherapy (OIT).22,59–62 It is time consuming for clinicians and requires significant commitment for families.

chunks.text:
A Cochrane review in 2018 commented that studies were small, and the quality of evidence is low.63,64 There are no standardized protocols and a high incidence of adverse events.63,65 In one study, adrenaline was required in 26% of children.65 Early discontinuation is associated with underlying asthma, higher specific IgE and lower threshold during double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge.65 Ovomucoid IgE >8.85 kU/L indicated a 95% probability of early discontinuation or ongoing reactions over time.65

More recent protocols achieve tolerance in 50% of patients.60,66 The benefits are sustained for up to 5 years after treatment.66 Daily dosing is more effective than weekly dosing.67 Low pre-treatment levels of egg white and ovomucoid IgE predict sustained unresponsiveness following egg immunotherapy.68 Decrease in size of SPT and increase in egg-specific IgG4 over time predicts tolerance in children being treated with egg OIT.61 Ovalbumin IgG4 and Ovalbumin IgE/ IgG4 ratio may be useful to predict the development of tolerance to egg in oral immunotherapy.65

EAACI does not currently recommend egg OIT as a treatment to achieve long-term tolerance in children with persistent egg allergy.69 Egg oral immunotherapy should only be undertaken in highly specialized allergy centres.69

#### 11.2 | Egg allergy as a risk factor for peanut allergy

Infants with egg allergy are at risk of developing peanut allergy. The introduction of regular high-dose peanut into the diet of egg-allergic children under 11 months of age reduces the incidence of peanut allergy at 5 years of age.25 Introduction of peanut in children with egg allergy is discussed in the BSACI Early weaning guidance.78 Infants undergoing SPT or measurement of specific IgE to egg proteins should also be tested for peanut sensitization, and peanut containing food introduced alongside other solid foods from around 6 months of age. #### 11.3 | Egg allergy and Eosinophilic oesophagitis

Children and adults with eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) respond to elimination of common food allergens, including egg.79 Cow's milk and wheat are the most likely triggers of EoE, but a large multicentre study of both children and adults reported that 15% of the subjects had reactions to egg.79 Egg may be a relevant trigger in 35% of children and 26–36% of adults.80–82 Egg avoidance is usually included as part of an empiric four or six food elimination diet.79 Egg SPT is a poor predictor of egg as a trigger for EoE.83

EoE has been reported as a complication of egg immunotherapy. This is usually reversible after early diagnosis and stopping the immunotherapy product.84 There is no evidence that home introduction of egg will cause EoE.

#### 11.4 | Use of Propofol in egg-allergic patients

A commonly used formulation of Propofol contains egg lecithin, derived from egg yolk. Propofol administration is safe in adult patients with egg allergy, or who are sensitized to egg.80,85 In a study of propofol administration in egg-allergic children, one child with anaphylaxis to egg developed urticaria and erythema on two occasions after the administration of propofol.86 Propofol is safe to use in children with egg allergy,.87,88

#### 11.5 | FPIES to egg

Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is a rare form of severe delayed type food allergy, thought to be non-IgE mediated, that leads to recurrent vomiting, fluid loss, dehydration, and shock, normally within 4 h of ingestion.89 Egg is a common food trigger for FPIES both in the UK and elsewhere,90 30% of infants with milk or soya FPIES also react to egg protein.91 The diagnosis is made on clinical history. #### 12.4 | Rabies vaccine

Rabies is a serious viral infection with a high case fatality rate.
